CAL/OSHA INJURY AND ILLNESS RECORDING REQUIREMENTS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INJURY AND ILLNESS RECORDING REQUIREMENTS INFORMATION SHEET
This Cal/OSHA Injury and Illness Recording Requirements — Information Sheet describes California's workplace injury and illness recordkeeping regulations, set out at 8 Cal. Code Regs. §§ 14300–14300.48, and the separate serious-injury-and-illness reporting regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 342, as those requirements relate to the working relationship between Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc.

It summarizes selected requirements of those regulations: what makes a workplace injury or illness “recordable” and the basic duty to record it on the Cal/OSHA Form 300 log, the partial exemption from routine recordkeeping available to some smaller employers and some lower-hazard industries, how long recorded records must be kept, the annual summary that must be created, certified, and posted each year, and the separate, more time-sensitive duty to report a serious injury, illness, or death to the Division of Occupational Safety and Health directly.

This topic is distinct from this corpus's Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP) — Information Sheet, which describes California's general written workplace-safety-program requirement under Labor Code § 6401.7 and 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 — a forward-looking duty to identify, evaluate, and correct workplace hazards — rather than the after-the-fact duty addressed here to record, and for serious cases report, a workplace injury or illness that has already occurred.

Acme, Inc. has identified Pat Morgan as the person responsible for injury and illness recordkeeping matters described in this information sheet.

This information sheet is not itself Acme, Inc.'s Cal/OSHA Form 300 log or Cal/OSHA Form 300A annual summary, does not itself satisfy 8 Cal. Code Regs. §§ 14300–14300.48's or § 342's requirements, and does not determine that any particular practice of Acme, Inc.'s is or is not compliant with California law.

THE BASIC DUTY TO RECORD AND WHAT MAKES AN INJURY OR ILLNESS RECORDABLE
The purpose section of California's Cal/OSHA recordkeeping regulation states directly that its purpose is to require employers to record work-related fatalities, injuries, and illnesses, and that recording a case does not by itself mean the employer or employee was at fault, that a Cal/OSHA regulation was violated, or that the employee is eligible for workers' compensation or other benefits. The regulation's general recording criteria section then states the operative test: an injury or illness must be considered recordable if it results in death, one or more days away from work, restricted work or transfer to another job, medical treatment beyond first aid, or loss of consciousness. Separately, a case must also be considered recordable — even without any of those five outcomes — if it involves a significant injury or illness diagnosed by a physician or other licensed health care professional; the regulation names cancer, a chronic irreversible disease, a fractured or cracked bone, and a punctured eardrum as examples that must always be recorded at the time of diagnosis on that basis.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The purpose of this rule (Article 2) is to require employers to record work-related fatalities, injuries and illnesses."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/14300.html)
  "You must consider an injury or illness to meet the general recording criteria, and therefore to be recordable, if it results in any of the following as detailed in subsections (b)(2) through (b)(6) of this section: death, days away from work, restricted work or transfer to another job, medical treatment beyond first aid, or loss of consciousness."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.7 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.7, subd. (a) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/14300_7.html)
  "Work-related cases involving cancer, chronic irreversible disease, a fractured or cracked bone, or a punctured eardrum must always be recorded under the general criteria at the time of diagnosis by a physician or other licensed health care professional."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.7 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.7, subd. (b)(7) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/14300_7.html)
  Known gap: Both citations below are drawn from the same regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. §§ 14300 and 14300.7, which are consecutively numbered sections of the same article (Article 2, Chapter 7) adopted together in the same 2002 rulemaking — they are not independent sources from one another. This clause does not independently verify the regulation's more detailed, category-specific recording criteria for particular injury types — for example, its separate provisions on needlestick and sharps injuries (§ 14300.8), work-related musculoskeletal disorders (§ 14300.12), or hearing loss, tuberculosis, or medical removal cases — or its definitions of “medical treatment” and “first aid” found later in § 14300.7(b)(5); those are not summarized here and no citation is offered for their specific terms. This is a description of what the regulation requires in general, not a determination that any particular injury or illness is or is not recordable.

THE PARTIAL EXEMPTION FROM ROUTINE RECORDKEEPING FOR SMALL EMPLOYERS AND CERTAIN INDUSTRIES
The recordkeeping regulation states two separate partial exemptions from the duty to keep the Cal/OSHA Form 300 log. The first is based on company size: if a company had ten (10) or fewer employees at all times during the last calendar year, it does not need to keep Cal/OSHA injury and illness records unless OSHA or the Bureau of Labor Statistics informs it in writing that records must be kept under specified government-request provisions. The regulation's own implementation guidance states that this size-based exemption is measured by the number of employees in the entire company — based on the company's peak employment during the last calendar year — not by the number of employees at any single establishment. The second exemption is based on industry classification: an employer whose business establishment is classified in one of the specific industry groups listed in a table of North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes does not need to keep Cal/OSHA injury and illness records for that establishment, again unless the government makes a written request for records under the same government-request provisions. Unlike the size-based exemption, the industry-based exemption applies establishment by establishment: a company with several establishments in different lines of business may have some establishments that must keep records and others that are exempt. Both provisions state, in the same sentence granting the exemption, that the exemption does not affect the separate duty to report a serious injury, illness, or death directly to the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, addressed in a companion clause of this information sheet.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "If your company had ten (10) or fewer employees at all times during the last calendar year, you do not need to keep Cal/OSHA injury and illness records unless OSHA or the BLS informs you in writing that you must keep records under the provisions of Section 14300.41 or Section 14300.42. However, all employers must continue to file reports of occupational injuries and illnesses with the Division of Labor Statistics and Research as required by Article 1 of this subchapter, and to immediately report to the Division of Occupational Safety and Health any workplace incident that results in serious injury or illness, or death, as required by Title 8 Section 342."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.1 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.1, subd. (a)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/14300_1.html)
  "The partial exemption for size is based on the number of employees in the entire company."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.1 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.1, subd. (b)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/14300_1.html)
  "If you are an employer and your business establishment is classified in a specific industry group listed in Table 1 in Appendix A of this section, you do not need to keep Cal/OSHA injury and illness records required by Article 2 unless the government asks you to keep the records under Section 14300.41 or Section 14300.42. However, all employers must report to the Division of Occupational Safety and Health any workplace incident that results in a serious injury or illness, or death, as required at Title 8 Section 342."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.2 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.2, subd. (a)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/14300_2.html)
  "The partial industry classification exemption applies to individual business establishments. If a company has several business establishments engaged in different classes of business activities, some of the company's establishments may be required to keep records, while others may be partially exempt."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.2 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.2, subd. (b)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/14300_2.html)
  Known gap: The two citations below are drawn from two separate, consecutively numbered sections of the same article, 8 Cal. Code Regs. §§ 14300.1 and 14300.2 — both adopted in the same 2002 rulemaking under the same statutory authority (Labor Code § 6410) — and are not independent sources from one another. This clause does not independently reproduce the industry table itself (Table 1 in Appendix A to § 14300.2), which the fetched text confirms exists and lists specific NAICS codes and industry names (for example, several retail, information, real estate, and professional-services categories), but which is too long to quote here in full; no representation is made about whether any particular NAICS code is or is not on that list beyond what is quoted below. This clause also does not independently verify the government-request provisions, 8 Cal. Code Regs. §§ 14300.41 and 14300.42, that can override either exemption; they are named here only as topics the regulation itself cross-references, not as verified content.

HOW LONG RECORDED INJURY AND ILLNESS RECORDS MUST BE KEPT
For an employer that is not exempt from routine recordkeeping, the regulation requires the Cal/OSHA Form 300 log, the privacy case list (if one exists), the Cal/OSHA Form 300A annual summary, and the Cal/OSHA Form 301 Incident Reports to be saved for five years following the end of the calendar year the records cover. During that five-year storage period, the regulation requires the stored Form 300 log itself to be updated to include newly discovered recordable injuries or illnesses and to reflect any change in the classification of a previously recorded case, but it does not require the stored annual summary (Form 300A) or the stored incident reports (Form 301) to be updated, though an employer may choose to do so.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "You must save the Cal/OSHA Form 300, the privacy case list (if one exists), the Cal/OSHA Form 300A, and the Cal/OSHA Form 301 Incident Reports for five (5) years following the end of the calendar year that these records cover."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.33 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.33, subd. (a) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/14300_33.html)
  "During the storage period, you must update your stored Cal/OSHA 300 forms to include newly discovered recordable injuries or illnesses and to show any changes that have occurred in the classification of previously recorded injuries and illnesses."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.33 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.33, subd. (b)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/14300_33.html)
  Known gap: Both citations below are drawn from the same regulatory section, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.33, subdivisions (a) and (b)(1) — not independent sources from one another. This five-year retention period is a different figure from, and should not be confused with, the one-year retention period this corpus's Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP) — Information Sheet describes for a written IIPP's inspection and training records under the separate regulation 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203(b); the two regulations impose distinct retention duties for distinct categories of records. This clause does not independently verify § 14300.33(b)(2) or (b)(3), which state that updating the Form 300A and Form 301 is optional; those provisions are described in this clause's body based on the fetched text but are not separately quoted or cited.

THE ANNUAL SUMMARY: CREATION, CERTIFICATION, AND POSTING
At the end of each calendar year, the regulation requires a covered employer to review the Cal/OSHA Form 300 log for completeness and accuracy, create an annual summary of the recorded cases using the Cal/OSHA Form 300A, certify that summary, and post it. The certification must be made by a “company executive” as the regulation defines that term, who must certify having examined the Form 300 and reasonably believing, based on knowledge of how the information was recorded, that the annual summary is correct and complete. The completed, certified summary must then be posted in each establishment in a conspicuous place or places where notices to employees are customarily posted, without alteration, defacement, or being covered by other material, and the regulation fixes the posting window itself: no later than February 1 of the year following the year the records cover, with the posting kept in place until April 30.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "At the end of each calendar year, you must:
(1) Review the Cal/OSHA Form 300 to verify that the entries are complete and accurate, and correct any deficiencies identified;
(2) Create an annual summary of injuries and illnesses recorded on the Cal/OSHA Form 300 using the Cal/OSHA Form 300A Annual Summary of Work-related Injuries and Illnesses;
(3) Certify the annual summary; and
(4) Post the annual summary."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.32 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.32, subd. (a) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/14300_32.html)
  "A company executive must certify that he or she has examined the Cal/OSHA Form 300 and that he or she reasonably believes, based on his or her knowledge of the process by which the information was recorded, that the annual summary is correct and complete."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.32 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.32, subd. (b)(3) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/14300_32.html)
  "You must post a copy of the annual summary in each establishment in a conspicuous place or places where notices to employees are customarily posted. You must ensure that the posted annual summary is not altered, defaced or covered by other material."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.32 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.32, subd. (b)(5) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/14300_32.html)
  "You must post the annual summary no later than February 1 of the year following the year covered by the records and keep the posting in place until April 30."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.32 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.32, subd. (b)(6) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/14300_32.html)
  Known gap: All three citations below are drawn from the same regulatory section, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.32, subdivisions (a), (b)(3), (b)(5), and (b)(6) — not independent sources from one another. This clause does not independently quote § 14300.32(b)(4), which lists the four categories of person who may qualify as the “company executive” permitted to certify the summary (an owner, a corporate officer, the highest-ranking company official at the establishment, or that official's immediate supervisor); it is described in this clause's body based on the fetched text but not separately cited. This clause also does not address § 14300.32(b)(7)'s separate requirement to present or mail the summary to employees who do not normally report to a posting location, or § 14300.32(b)(8)'s treatment of closed establishments; those provisions are not summarized here. This clause describes the general annual-summary duty for a non-exempt employer, not whether any specific employer's summary was in fact prepared, certified, or posted as required.

THE SEPARATE DUTY TO REPORT A SERIOUS INJURY, ILLNESS, OR DEATH DIRECTLY TO CAL/OSHA
Apart from the routine Form 300 recordkeeping duty addressed in the other clauses of this information sheet, a separate Cal/OSHA regulation — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 342, found in a different chapter of Title 8 that governs Cal/OSHA's own reporting and enforcement procedures rather than in the recordkeeping article — requires every employer to report immediately to the Division of Occupational Safety and Health any serious injury or illness, or death, of an employee occurring in a place of employment or in connection with any employment, by telephone or through a specified online mechanism the Division has established for that purpose. The regulation defines “immediately” with a specific outer limit: as soon as practically possible, but not longer than 8 hours after the employer knows, or with diligent inquiry would have known, of the death or serious injury or illness — extended to not longer than 24 hours after the incident only if the employer can demonstrate that exigent circumstances exist. This duty applies without regard to whether the employer is otherwise partially exempt from routine Form 300 recordkeeping under the size-based or industry-based exemptions addressed in a companion clause of this information sheet; the recordkeeping regulation's own cross-reference restates the same reporting duty in shorthand, requiring a report “within eight (8) hours,” as required by § 342. “Serious injury or illness” is itself a defined term, found in a companion section of the same reporting-procedure chapter: an injury or illness occurring in a place of employment or in connection with any employment that requires inpatient hospitalization for other than medical observation or diagnostic testing, or in which an employee suffers an amputation, the loss of an eye, or any serious degree of permanent disfigurement — excluding, with one exception, an injury, illness, or death caused by an accident on a public street or highway, the exception being an accident that occurred in a construction zone.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Every employer shall report immediately to the Division of Occupational Safety and Health any serious injury or illness, or death, of an employee occurring in a place of employment or in connection with any employment. The report shall be made by the telephone or through a specified online mechanism established by the Division for this purpose."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 342 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 342, subd. (a) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/342.html)
  "Immediately means as soon as practically possible but not longer than 8 hours after the employer knows or with diligent inquiry would have known of the death or serious injury or illness. If the employer can demonstrate that exigent circumstances exist, the time frame for the report may be made no longer than 24 hours after the incident."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 342 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 342, subd. (a) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/342.html)
  "“Serious injury or illness” means any injury or illness occurring in a place of employment or in connection with any employment that requires inpatient hospitalization for other than medical observation or diagnostic testing, or in which an employee suffers an amputation, the loss of an eye, or any serious degree of permanent disfigurement, but does not include any injury or illness or death caused by an accident on a public street or highway, unless the accident occurred in a construction zone."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 330 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 330, subd. (h) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/330.html)
  "You must also report any work-related fatality or serious injury or illness to the Division of Occupational Safety and Health within eight (8) hours, as required by Title 8 Section 342."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.7 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.7, subd. (b)(2) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/14300_7.html)
  Known gap: The citations to 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 342 and § 330 are independent of the citations to the § 14300 series elsewhere in this information sheet in the sense that §§ 342 and 330 sit in a different chapter of Title 8 (Chapter 3.2, the Cal/OSHA regulations governing the Division of Occupational Safety and Health's own procedures) from the recordkeeping regulation's Chapter 7, Article 2, and were adopted separately (§ 342 originally in 1974, § 330(h) most recently amended in 2020); they are not, however, independent of each other, since both are sections of the same Article 3 (§ 342) and Article 1 (§ 330) of that same chapter, and the § 342 citations (the two paragraphs of subdivision (a)) are two sentences of the same subdivision. The quotation from 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.7(b)(2) is drawn from the same regulation cited in this information sheet's recording-criteria clause and is not an independent source. The regulation's own text of § 330(h), as currently in force, does not state a minimum duration of inpatient hospitalization (such as a 24-hour minimum stay) as a condition of the definition; this document did not fetch or verify the parallel federal OSHA serious-injury-and-illness reporting regulation, 29 C.F.R. § 1904.39, so no comparison is made here between California's definition or 8-hour/24-hour reporting timeline and any federal counterpart, and the two should not be assumed identical. This clause does not independently verify § 342(c)'s list of information a report should include, or § 342(b)'s separate notification duty for responding fire or police agencies; those are not summarized here.

expectedJSON.body: At the end of each calendar year, the regulation requires a covered employer to review the Cal/OSHA Form 300 log for completeness and accuracy, create an annual summary of the recorded cases using the Cal/OSHA Form 300A, certify that summary, and post it. The certification must be made by a “company executive” as the regulation defines that term, who must certify having examined the Form 300 and reasonably believing, based on knowledge of how the information was recorded, that the annual summary is correct and complete. The completed, certified summary must then be posted in each establishment in a conspicuous place or places where notices to employees are customarily posted, without alteration, defacement, or being covered by other material, and the regulation fixes the posting window itself: no later than February 1 of the year following the year the records cover, with the posting kept in place until April 30.

expectedJSON.body: Apart from the routine Form 300 recordkeeping duty addressed in the other clauses of this information sheet, a separate Cal/OSHA regulation — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 342, found in a different chapter of Title 8 that governs Cal/OSHA's own reporting and enforcement procedures rather than in the recordkeeping article — requires every employer to report immediately to the Division of Occupational Safety and Health any serious injury or illness, or death, of an employee occurring in a place of employment or in connection with any employment, by telephone or through a specified online mechanism the Division has established for that purpose. The regulation defines “immediately” with a specific outer limit: as soon as practically possible, but not longer than 8 hours after the employer knows, or with diligent inquiry would have known, of the death or serious injury or illness — extended to not longer than 24 hours after the incident only if the employer can demonstrate that exigent circumstances exist. This duty applies without regard to whether the employer is otherwise partially exempt from routine Form 300 recordkeeping under the size-based or industry-based exemptions addressed in a companion clause of this information sheet; the recordkeeping regulation's own cross-reference restates the same reporting duty in shorthand, requiring a report “within eight (8) hours,” as required by § 342. “Serious injury or illness” is itself a defined term, found in a companion section of the same reporting-procedure chapter: an injury or illness occurring in a place of employment or in connection with any employment that requires inpatient hospitalization for other than medical observation or diagnostic testing, or in which an employee suffers an amputation, the loss of an eye, or any serious degree of permanent disfigurement — excluding, with one exception, an injury, illness, or death caused by an accident on a public street or highway, the exception being an accident that occurred in a construction zone.

If the employer can demonstrate that exigent circumstances exist, the time frame for the report may be made no longer than 24 hours after the incident.

The quotation from 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.7(b)(2) is drawn from the same regulation cited in this information sheet's recording-criteria clause and is not an independent source. The regulation's own text of § 330(h), as currently in force, does not state a minimum duration of inpatient hospitalization (such as a 24-hour minimum stay) as a condition of the definition; this document did not fetch or verify the parallel federal OSHA serious-injury-and-illness reporting regulation, 29 C.F.R. § 1904.39, so no comparison is made here between California's definition or 8-hour/24-hour reporting timeline and any federal counterpart, and the two should not be assumed identical.
